what: How each aircraft type the game can draw or the rules can name really flew: size, weight, power, speeds and heights, climb, turn, roll, g, dive, load and range, each figure with its source and how sure it is; and how each air force fought, by nation and year. Read by Battle/AirPerf (no engine), which gives the 3D flight core its limits in its own units.
asked: Brian, 24 Nov 2026: "i want the flying to be smooth and very realistic" and "i want the planes flying with realistic capabilities and tactics".
sure: Every figure is [value, source, mark] or [value, source, mark, low, high]. Marks: measured (a flight trial's figure), manufacturer (the maker's or the service's published figure), derived (computed here, or a stand-in's mean), uncertain (a range; the value is the middle the historian would bet on). Set from knowledge by the historian on 25 Nov 2026: only the pages named 'read' in the sources were read that day, and a figure marked measured or manufacturer is the figure as commonly reproduced, not checked against the document. Fixed on 25 Nov 2026 after review: no figure is credited to a source that was not read for it (Ackroyd and Lamont's, the AFDU's, Gordon's for German types), the quoted stalls checked against their lift, and a tactic is a fact only with a historical source beside doctrine.ts.

units.mass_kg: the weight it fought at (normal loaded)
units.power_hp: all engines' horsepower at power_m metres (its rated height; a two-stage engine's high gear)
units.thrust_kn: a jet's static thrust at sea level, all engines
units.top_kmh: top level speed at top_m metres, true
units.cruise_kmh: the speed it cruised at on operations, true
units.stall_kmh: stalling speed, clean, power off, indicated, as the pilot's notes give it (the indicator reads low near the stall: a lift of 1.2 to 1.8 at the row's weight). A cross-check only: AirPerf works its stall out from its weight, its wing and the lift it turns with
units.turn_m: a documented sustained turn's radius at turn_at_m
units.turn_s: a documented time for a full sustained turn at turn_at_m
units.roll_dps: peak rate of roll, degrees a second, at roll_kmh indicated
units.roll_fast_dps: the rate of roll at roll_fast_kmh indicated
units.bomb_kg: a usual bomb or torpedo load
units.power_low_hp: a two-speed or two-stage supercharger's low gear: all engines' horsepower at power_low_m metres (where given)
units.clmax: the lift coefficient usable in a hard turn, where given (else a plain wing's 1.35)
units.stall_flaps_kmh: a quoted stalling speed whose lift at the row's weight (over 1.8) says it is not a clean stall: most likely flaps and wheels down, often at landing weight. Kept as quoted; not used
units.models: the row's plain model names (as the scene and the rules name the 3D model): only these walk the marks by date; a mark named outright flies as named
units.marks: the row to fly from each year on, for a plain model name (the record's dates; where guns.ts differs, its notes say)

sources.std: The standard published figures for the type: the maker's and the service's figures as reproduced in the standard references (Jane's Fighting Aircraft of World War II; Green and Swanborough's fact files). Set from knowledge on 25 Nov 2026, not checked against a page.
sources.rules: The rules' own data/aircraft.json (release 2's documented figures for six types), read on 25 Nov 2026; kept where this table agrees with it.
sources.francillon: Francillon, Japanese Aircraft of the Pacific War (Putnam, 1970 and 1979): the Japanese makers' and services' figures. From knowledge, not read on the page.
sources.gordon: Gordon and Khazanov, Soviet Combat Aircraft of the Second World War (Midland, 1998-99), giving NII VVS state-trial figures of the Soviet types. From knowledge, not read on the page; used for the Soviet rows only.
sources.aaee: A&AEE (Martlesham Heath, later Boscombe Down) performance trials of the type, as commonly reproduced. From knowledge, not read on the page.
sources.rae109: RAE Farnborough flight trials of the captured Bf 109E (Morgan and Morris, 1940): heavy ailerons at speed, and turning circles calculated from the trials (Bf 109E 885 ft radius at 12,000 ft against the Spitfire I's 696 ft). As commonly quoted; not read on the page.
sources.afdu190: AFDU Duxford, tactical trials of the captured Fw 190A-3 against the Spitfire VB, report of August 1942: the Fw 190 faster by 25 to 35 mph at all heights, markedly better in climb, dive and rate of roll, better in acceleration; the Spitfire turns tighter. Findings read on 25 Nov 2026 in a summary (History Hit, 'The Spitfire V or the Fw190'). Comparisons only: no absolute figure in this table is credited to it.
sources.akutan: US Navy flight tests of the captured Akutan Zero (Sanders, 20 Sep to 15 Oct 1942), published in Informational Intelligence Summary 59 and 85: ailerons 'froze up' above 200 knots, it rolled left more easily than right, the engine cut under negative g; advice to dive, push over, and roll hard right at about 200 knots. Read on 25 Nov 2026 in Wikipedia 'Akutan Zero', citing Rearden, Koga's Zero, p. 73.
sources.taic: TAIC (Technical Air Intelligence Center) comparative trials of a captured A6M5 against US fighters, 1944; the report's number not checked. From knowledge.
sources.naca868: Toll, NACA Report 868, Summary of lateral-control research (1947). Its text, read on 25 Nov 2026 (ntrs.nasa.gov 19930090943), names only the P-47C-1-RE (wing twist costs 31 per cent of its aileron effectiveness at 400 mph IAS), the Spitfire (about 65 per cent at 400 mph IAS) and the XP-51 (pb/2V about doubled under 300 mph by its new ailerons). The many-fighter roll chart often credited to it was not found in its text.
sources.rollchart: The wartime comparison of fighters' rates of roll at 10,000 ft with a 50 lb stick force (NACA flight measurements, compiled in Dean, America's Hundred Thousand, 1997, graph 81, as a forum post read on 25 Nov 2026 cites it). Values recalled from the chart, not read: marked uncertain with a range.
sources.ackroyd: Ackroyd and Lamont, A comparison of the turning radii of four Battle of Britain fighter aircraft, The Aeronautical Journal 104 (1032), February 2000, pp. 53-58: an analysis from published flight data of the Spitfire, Hurricane, Bf 109E and Bf 110. Abstract read on 25 Nov 2026 (twice: it gives no radii and no ranking); its figures were not read, so no figure in this table is taken from it.
sources.notes: The type's own pilot's notes or pilot's flight operating instructions (its placard limits). From knowledge, not read on the page.
sources.lundstrom: Lundstrom, The First Team (1984) and The First Team and the Guadalcanal Campaign (1994): the US Navy's fighters, tactics and losses against the Zero. From knowledge.
sources.mcfarland: McFarland and Newton, To Command the Sky: the Battle for Air Superiority over Germany, 1942-1944 (1991). From knowledge.
sources.hardesty: Hardesty, Red Phoenix: the Rise of Soviet Air Power 1941-1945 (1982; with Grinberg as Red Phoenix Rising, 2012). From knowledge.
sources.galland: Galland, The First and the Last (1954): the Luftwaffe's fighter arm, the Rotte and Schwarm, the free hunt and the close-escort orders of 1940. From knowledge.
sources.murray: Murray, Strategy for Defeat: the Luftwaffe 1933-1945 (1983), read in part by the historian on 24 Nov 2026 (historian/air-reads-1124.md).
sources.historian: The historian's readings of 24 Nov 2026 in this project (historian/air-reads-1124.md and air-reads-2-1124.md).
sources.doctrine: The rules' src/battle/air/doctrine.ts (the design's table 1.2 and its claim ids D, B and E, checked by the historian's review), read on 25 Nov 2026.
sources.estimate: An estimate made in this pass (25 Nov 2026) where no published figure was found or read, always marked uncertain, with a range. The turning lift of a slatted or flapped wing is reasoned in its row's notes. The rates of roll not on the wartime chart (rollchart) nor in a trial are judged from size, weight and the reputation of the ailerons, against the charted fighters: the bombers', dive bombers', torpedo bombers' and the Fulmar's; the Soviet, Italian, French and smaller air forces' fighters', the Ki-43's and the Me 262's; and every fighter's rate at high speed where the chart's fall was not recalled.
sources.derived: Derived here: computed from the row's other figures by the formulas in Battle/AirPerf.h, or, for a stand-in, the rounded mean of the types it stands for.
sources.niivvs: The NII VVS (the Soviet air force's research institute) trials of captured German fighters, 1942-43 (a Bf 109F, a Bf 109G-2, an Fw 190A-4), whose times for a full turn at 1,000 m are commonly quoted in later secondary works. Recalled, not read, and the report not identified: every figure from it is marked uncertain.
sources.wikimerlin: Wikipedia, 'Rolls-Royce Merlin', its list of variants, read on 25 Nov 2026: the Merlin 61 '1,565 hp at 3,000 rpm at 12,250 ft (3,730 m), 1,390 hp at 3,000 rpm at 23,500 ft (7,163 m)' (the maker's ratings as reproduced).

rows.style_why: Out-turned the Bf 109E (the RAE's calculation from its trials) and could dive with it; RAF pilots turned with the 109 and took the escorts while the Hurricanes took the bombers.
rows.notes: The 3D model is a Mk I. A plain 'Spitfire' flies the mark of its date: the V from 1941 (guns.ts's VB), the IX from 1943. The IX's date is a reading: it reached its first squadron, No. 64, in July 1942, but the V was most of Fighter Command's Spitfires to the end of 1942. guns.ts arms a 1942 Spitfire as the 'IX (C wing)': the same guns as the VC's C wing, so the two agree.

rows.style_why: Metal ailerons rolled better than the Mk I's fabric; out-turned the Bf 109F and the Fw 190A but was out-climbed, out-dived and out-rolled by the Fw 190 (AFDU, August 1942).
Matched the Fw 190A in speed and climb at most heights and out-turned it; flown both ways from late 1942.
rows.notes: Its two-stage Merlin 61's two ratings (read on 25 Nov 2026): 1,565 hp at 3,730 m in its low gear, 1,390 hp at 7,163 m in its high gear; the Merlin 63 and 66 of later IXs gave more.

rows.style_why: A Spitfire for the deck, flown as the Spitfire was; clipped wings for the low-level fight over the fleet.
A steady gun platform with a thick wing that turned tightly; slower than the Bf 109E, it was set on the bombers while the Spitfires fought the escort (Fighter Command, 1940).
rows.notes: Its turn_m (245 m at 3,660 m, 220 to 260) was credited to Ackroyd and Lamont, whose figures were not read: it is kept as an unsourced estimate, marked uncertain, as a cross-check only. What is flown is the worked-out turn (about 219 m at 3,000 m).

rows.style_why: A slow two-seat deck fighter with eight guns and long range: good against shadowers and bombers, never a match for single-seat fighters.
A light day bomber in vics of three; lost heavily by day to fighters and flak (1940-41).
Geodetic, tough and slow; flown by day in vics until the Heligoland Bight (18 December 1939) sent Bomber Command to night bombing.
Night bomber in the bomber stream; when a night fighter was seen, the corkscrew: a diving turn, a climbing turn the other way, over and over.

Pairs and fours diving from height, one pass and zoom away (Mölders' Rotte and Schwarm, Spain 1937-38); out-climbed the Hurricane and dived well, but its pilots were taught never to turn with Spitfires or Hurricanes: heavy ailerons at speed, a wider turn (RAE).
rows.notes: The 3D model is a Bf 109E. A plain 'Bf109' flies the mark of its date: the F from 1941, the G from mid-1942 (a reading of the date: the G-2 replaced the F-4 in the Jagdgeschwader from about June 1942). guns.ts arms a 'Bf109' as the F-4 from 1941 to the end: the G-2's guns were the F-4's (one MG 151/20 and two MG 17), but the G-6's two MG 131 of 1943-45 are not in guns.ts (a question for the rules, not for this table). The usable lift in a hard turn (clmax 1.45, against a plain wing's 1.35) is this pass's estimate for its automatic leading-edge slats, which let it pull nearer the stall without dropping a wing; no measured figure was read.

rows.style_why: The cleanest 109: fast, a fine climber, flown in the climb and dive by the Schwarm; still not a turning fighter against the Spitfire V.
rows.notes: The usable lift in a hard turn (clmax 1.45, against a plain wing's 1.35) is this pass's estimate for its automatic leading-edge slats, which let it pull nearer the stall without dropping a wing; no measured figure was read.

rows.style_why: Heavier than the F, faster at height, worse in the turn; the Schwarm's climb and dive, and from 1943 the top cover over the Sturmgruppen.
rows.notes: One row for the G-2 to the G-14, its figures the G-6's (the G-2 of 1942 was a little lighter and faster, the G-14 of 1944 a little faster with its boost). The usable lift in a hard turn (clmax 1.45, against a plain wing's 1.35) is this pass's estimate for its automatic leading-edge slats, which let it pull nearer the stall without dropping a wing; no measured figure was read.

rows.style_why: Too heavy to turn with single-seat fighters: a long-range escort and bomber destroyer, falling back on the defensive circle when bounced (1940); with rockets against the American boxes in 1943.
rows.notes: Its turn_m (320 m at 3,660 m, 290 to 360) was credited to Ackroyd and Lamont, whose figures were not read: it is kept as an unsourced estimate, marked uncertain, as a cross-check only. What is flown is the worked-out turn (about 313 m at 3,000 m).

rows.style_why: Faster, better in the climb and dive and far better in the roll than the Spitfire V; flicked into a reversal or a dive the Spitfire could not follow; the Spitfire turned tighter (AFDU, August 1942).
rows.notes: The 3D model is an Fw 190A; the A-8 from 1944, as guns.ts. Its BMW 801D-2 gave more power low in its first supercharger gear (about 1,580 PS, 1,560 hp, near 1,700 m) than its rated 1,440 PS at 5,700 m; power_low is that, recalled, not read.

rows.style_why: Armoured and heavy: the Sturmgruppen's bomber killer closing to 100 m astern in line abreast, and from 1944 the fighter-bomber that took the Stuka's place.
Fastest in the sky but slow to accelerate and wide in the turn: struck bombers from astern at speed in threes and climbed away; never turned with piston fighters.
rows.notes: The usable lift in a hard turn (clmax 1.45, against a plain wing's 1.35) is this pass's estimate for its automatic leading-edge slats, which let it pull nearer the stall without dropping a wing; no measured figure was read. Its sustained turn at 3,000 m works out at about 450 to 500 m: the widest of the fighters, as its pilots found.

rows.style_why: The Luftwaffe's main level bomber: Ketten of three, Staffeln of three Ketten in a wedge, the escort close above from late August 1940.
Fast bomber that could dive at 60 degrees with brakes; the Luftwaffe's best twin, also a night fighter.
The 'flying pencil': flown low and level, and at low level against airfields in August 1940.

Dive bomber: from about 4,000 m it rolled into a 60 to 90 degree dive with its brakes out, let go at 450 to 700 m and pulled out at about 6 g, often by its automatic pull-out; deadly where the enemy's fighters were absent.
Out-dived and out-rolled the Zero and the Oscar and was tough; the AVG's rule (Chennault): hit, dive away, never turn with them.
Heavy and very fast in a dive: bounced from height and dived away, out-diving every German fighter; would not turn or climb with them low down; a fighter-bomber over France in 1944.
The long-range escort of early 1944: fast at height and in the dive; pairs and fours, boom and zoom; freed to hunt ahead of the bombers from January 1944.
rows.notes: Its V-1650-3's low-gear rating (about 1,550 hp near 3,800 m) is recalled, not read: an estimate with a range. The high gear's 1,300 hp at 8,500 m is the rated power.

rows.style_why: As the P-51B, with the bubble canopy and six guns; the escort that hunted the Luftwaffe's fighters in 1944-45.
rows.notes: The 3D model is a P-51D; a plain 'Mustang' flies the P-51B before June 1944, as guns.ts. Its V-1650-7's low-gear rating (about 1,590 hp near 2,600 m) is recalled, not read: an estimate with a range; the high gear's 1,500 hp at 5,900 m is the rated power.

rows.style_why: Fast and a fine climber, but slow to roll without boosted ailerons and caught by compressibility in a steep dive: in the Pacific it climbed and dived and never turned with the Zero.
Out-turned and out-climbed by the Zero: never dogfight it. Pairs and the Thach weave, a high-side pass and dive away; tough enough to live through the Zero's guns (Lundstrom).
Out-climbed and out-dived the Zero and could stay with it in a fast turn, where the Zero's ailerons stiffened; fought in pairs with the weave (TAIC's Zeke 52 trials).
Fast and a fine diver: the Marines' hit-and-run fighter over the Solomons from February 1943.
Day bomber of the Eighth Air Force's first year: the staggered group formations of late 1942 and the combat box of 1943; its thin nose defence drew the head-on attack from November 1942.
rows.notes: Stands for the B-17E and F of 1942-43: no chin turret, fewer guns and less armour than the G, so lighter, a little faster and higher. Its figures are recalled, not read (the E about 510 km/h at 25,000 ft, the F 480 to 523 km/h by source): each marked uncertain with its range; the rest as the G's row.

rows.style_why: Day bomber in the combat box of 1943 (18 to 21 aircraft stepped up and down for mutual fire); bombed on the lead's drop.
rows.notes: The 3D model is a G. A plain 'B17' flies the B-17F (standing for the E and F) to August 1943 and the G from September 1943, as guns.ts arms them; the guns by date are guns.ts's.

rows.style_why: Faster and longer-ranged than the B-17 but higher wing loading: worse at height and harder to hold in a tight box.
Pressurised and fast for its size: bombed Japan from 9,000 m in 1944, then low at night with fire from March 1945.
Dive bomber: from 4,000 to 6,000 m in a 70 degree dive with its split flaps open, letting go at 450 to 600 m; it sank four carriers at Midway.
Heavier and faster than the Dauntless, with an internal bay; the fleet's dive bomber from November 1943.
Slow torpedo bomber that had to fly low and slow to drop its Mk 13; unescorted at Midway, nearly all were lost.
The big, tough successor to the Devastator: torpedoes low and abreast, or bombs from a glide.
The plain patrol flying boat the sea scene draws for every navy: slow, long-ranged, a shadower and a bomber of submarines.

The best-turning fighter of 1941-42 at low and medium speed, flown by navy pilots of 500 hours and more: it drew its enemies into a slow turning fight. Above about 200 knots its ailerons stiffened and it rolled badly, its engine cut under negative g, and it could not follow a dive (Akutan Zero tests).
rows.notes: The 3D model is an A6M2; the marks by date follow guns.ts.

rows.style_why: As the A6M2 with more power; flown over Guadalcanal and New Guinea at the end of its range.
Shorter wings and a stronger skin for a faster dive, still out-turning the Hellcat at low speed but out-classed in speed, climb and dive by 1944 (TAIC's trials).
The army's agile turner, with combat flaps: it drew Allied fighters into slow turns, but was fragile and lightly armed.
rows.notes: The usable lift in a hard turn (clmax 1.45, against a plain wing's 1.35) is this pass's estimate for its butterfly combat flaps, lowered in a turning fight; no measured figure was read.

rows.style_why: The navy's long-range land bomber: chutai of nine in vics, bombing on the leader's drop from high, or torpedoes low (Prince of Wales and Repulse, 10 December 1941).
Fast and very long-ranged by giving up armour and self-sealing tanks: it burned easily. Big vees of 9 to 27 in tight formation; torpedoes low and abreast.
rows.notes: The marks by date follow guns.ts (the G4M2 from September 1943).

rows.style_why: As the G4M1 with more power and a gun turret above; still unarmoured.
Torpedo bomber that struck low from both bows at once (the anvil), or bombed level from about 3,000 m in vics (Pearl Harbor).
The Kate's faster successor from 1944, flown by crews of far less training.
Dive bomber: from 3,000 to 4,000 m in a 55 to 60 degree dive, letting go at about 450 m; the most accurate of 1941-42.
A fast dive bomber from 1944, as quick as many fighters.
Soviet fighters fought low, where the Yak's engine gave its best: tight threes, turning, under 4,000 m.
The Yak-1 with a clear canopy and more power low down; pairs and fours from late 1942 (doctrine.ts), Pokryshkin's 'height, speed, manoeuvre, fire'.
rows.notes: The 3D model is a Yak-1B; the marks by date follow guns.ts (Yak-1 to September 1942, the 1B to the end of 1942, the Yak-9 to mid-1944, the Yak-3 after).

rows.style_why: The commonest Soviet fighter of 1943-44: a match for the Bf 109G below 4,000 m, in the turn and the vertical.
Light and quick low down: out-turned and out-climbed the Bf 109G and Fw 190A under 4,000 m; the Normandie-Niemen's mount.
Fast and strong low down: Kozhedub's mount, fighting in the vertical and the turn under 5,000 m.
A high-altitude interceptor in a war fought low: fast above 5,000 m, heavy and slow to climb below it.
Short, stubby and unstable: quick to turn and roll, in tight threes low down; it could neither catch nor out-dive the Bf 109.
The armoured attack aircraft: small groups low over the front, and over the target the circle (the krug), each diving in turn at 25 to 30 degrees while the circle guarded his tail.
Fast twin that dived at 60 to 70 degrees with brakes; from 1943 Polbin's 'wheel' (the vertushka), each diving in turn.
Fast in 1936, outclassed by 1941: flown in tight vics, often unescorted, and lost in great numbers in June and July 1941.
Italian pilots, trained on the CR.42 biplane, liked the turning fight and fine flying; the C.200 was sturdy and well-mannered but slow and lightly armed.
A match for the Spitfire V and the P-40 over Malta and North Africa: turning but with height, in pairs and fours from 1942 (doctrine.ts).
Three-engined bomber in vics at 4,000 to 6,000 m over Malta; the Mediterranean's best torpedo bomber, attacking low in pairs.
France's best fighter of 1940: it could turn with and inside the Bf 109E; French patrols of three fought turning.
Slow and lightly armed but sturdy and agile: flown in tight patrols of three, turning, in 1939-40.
A fast, modern level bomber, thrown at the German columns at low level in May and June 1940, and lost heavily to flak.
The plain French bomber of 1939 (the Bloch MB.210 and the Amiot 143 alike): slow, flown at night or lost by day.

A gull-winged design of 1934, outpaced by the Bf 109 and even by the bombers: Polish pilots relied on the turn and on getting in close (the historian's read: about even against the Luftwaffe in September 1939, uncertain).
Fixed undercarriage, sturdy and agile: the Dutch fought turning in May 1940; the Finns in the Winter War flew pairs and fours and struck the bombers from height and below.
Light in Finnish hands: pairs and fours from height and out of the sun, with good sight and a good turn; Finnish records show 19 lost in combat in 1941-44 (the historian's read, likely).
Romania's own fighter from 1941: a fair match for the I-16 and the Hurricane, flown in German-style pairs and fours.
The plain fighter of 1939-41 (the P.11, D.XXI, MS.406, I-16 and C.200 it stands for): light, slow beside the Bf 109, turning.
rows.notes: The rounded mean of the P.11c, D.XXI, MS.406, I-16 type 24 and C.200 rows; the 3D model's span. CarrierFighter is the kit's plain carrier fighter, named by no rule today.

rows.style_why: The plain fighter from 1942 (as the IAR 80, C.202 and Yak-1): faster, and flown in pairs and fours.
rows.notes: The rounded mean of the IAR 80, C.202 and Yak-1 rows; the 3D model's span.

rows.style_why: The plain twin of 1939-41 (as the SB-2, Blenheim, MB.210 and He 111 it stands for).
rows.notes: The rounded mean of the SB-2, Blenheim IV, MB.210 and He 111H rows; the 3D model's span.

rows.style_why: A navy's plain carrier torpedo bomber (as the B5N, TBD and Swordfish it stands for).
rows.notes: The rounded mean of the B5N2, TBD-1 and Swordfish I rows; the shape's span.

rows.style_why: A navy's plain carrier dive bomber (as the SBD, D3A and Skua it stands for).
rows.notes: The rounded mean of the SBD-3, D3A1 and Skua II rows; the shape's span.

rows.style_why: A biplane torpedo bomber, slow enough that fighters overshot it: Taranto (11 November 1940) by night, the Bismarck's rudder (26 May 1941).
The Swordfish's successor: dive bomber against the Tirpitz (3 April 1944) as well as torpedo bomber.
The Fleet Air Arm's dive bomber and fighter of 1939-40: it sank the cruiser Konigsberg at Bergen (10 April 1940).

tactics.what: Fighters fly in the Rotte (a leader and his wingman, about 200 m apart) and the Schwarm (two Rotten, the 'finger four'), worked out in Spain in 1937-38; a Staffel is three Schwarme stepped up. The leader shoots; the wingman guards his tail.
Tight vics of three, sections in line astern, the Fighter Area Attacks by the book; one 'weaver' guarding the rear. Easy prey for a Schwarm diving from above.
Fours in line astern, then the 'fluid six'; finger fours (the German four) from about March 1941.
Two-ship elements, four-ship flights in finger four, 16-ship squadrons; boom and zoom from height.
Two-plane sections and four-plane divisions; the Thach weave: two sections turning toward each other whenever one is attacked, so the other's guns meet the attacker head-on.
The shotai of three (a leader and two wingmen in a loose vic), three shotai to a chutai; fours from 1943-44.
Ki-43 sentai flew threes like the navy, changing to fours in 1943.
The zveno of three in a tight vic, low and turning; from late 1942 pairs and fours; in 1943 Pokryshkin's 'height, speed, manoeuvre, fire' and fours stacked in height (the 'Kuban stairs').
Patrols of three in vics, turning; German pairs and fours with the C.202 from 1942.
Tight patrols of three, turning; the patrol attacked in turn from astern and the quarter.
Pairs and fours from the Winter War on, attacking from height, from the sun and from below.
The free hunt: Bf 109s swept ahead of the bombers, choosing their fight.
Goring's orders of 18 and 19 August tied the Bf 109s to the bombers: close escort weaving beside them, with top cover above; it cost the 109s their height and speed.
The Circus: a few bombers as bait under a close escort wing, an escort cover wing, high cover, and sweeps (Rodeos) and target-support wings around them.
Escorts tied to the bombers: close escort and top cover to the edge of their range (the P-47 to the German border), then the bombers went on alone.
Doolittle's order: destroy the German fighters. Groups swept ahead of the bombers and were freed to chase and to strafe airfields on the way home; relays of escorts along the route.
Close escort over the Il-2s, holding station (order 0685 of 9 September 1942): a fighter that left its Sturmoviks to chase was punished.
Top cover weaving above the bombers and, on big raids, a sweep ahead; not below the bombers.
Fighters crowded close round the SM.79s (over Malta).
From astern and the rear quarter, into the tail guns' and the box's crossfire.

Head-on from 12 o'clock level or a little high (Egon Mayer, JG 2, over St Nazaire): closing at 800 to 900 km/h, a burst of a second or two, then down and away under the box; the B-17's nose had few guns until the B-17G's chin turret.
Twin-engined destroyers (Bf 110G, Me 410) firing 21 cm rockets from about 1,000 m astern to break up a box, then picking off its stragglers; air-to-air bombs dropped on boxes from above.
The Sturmgruppen: armoured Fw 190A-8s in line abreast closing to about 100 m astern of a box, with Bf 109Gs above to hold off the escort.
Night fighters under ground control (Himmelbett), later free in the bomber stream (Zahme Sau, Wilde Sau); upward-firing guns (Schrage Musik) from below a Lancaster, which had no gun there.
Fighter Command's order: Hurricanes on the bombers, head-on where they could (few managed it), Spitfires on the escort.
Mostly head-on against the B-17 and B-24; against twins from astern and the quarter.
From the quarter astern and from below, under the dorsal gunner's arc; in 1941, sometimes by ramming (the taran).

tactics.who: Wildcat, P-40, P-38, P-39 v Zero and Oscar
tactics.what: Never dogfight a Zero or an Oscar below 300 knots: make one pass from height and dive away; roll right and dive at about 200 knots when one is on your tail (the Akutan tests).
The 109 climbs and dives; it does not turn with either at low speed.
The Spitfire must not try to dive or climb away from the Fw 190: it turns, and keeps its speed up.

tactics.who: Bf 109G and Fw 190A v Yak-3 and La-5FN
tactics.what: The German fighters fought from height and avoided turning with the Soviet fighters under 4,000 m; the Soviet fighters kept the fight low.
From height, dive, fire and zoom back up; never a slow turning or climbing fight low down.
Never turn: dive through at speed and climb away; most were lost taking off and landing, when they were slow.
The Zero must not follow them into a dive or fight them fast; its chance was the slow turn.
The combat box: 18 to 21 B-17s in three squadrons (lead, high and low) stepped up and down for mutual fire; three boxes to a combat wing of 54; bombing on the lead bombardier's drop.
Vics of three in sections; after the Heligoland Bight (18 December 1939) heavy bombers went to night bombing.
The bomber stream: no formation, each crew on its own route and time through a stream many miles long, over the target in a few minutes; the Lancaster's corkscrew when a night fighter was seen.
The Kette of three in a vic, Staffeln of three Ketten, the Gruppe in a wedge; in 1940 the escort close above and beside.
SBs in tight vics, often unescorted in 1941; Pe-2s in close vics that dived in turn; Il-2s in small groups low over the front.
Land bombers in big vees of 9 to 27 in tight formation, bombing together on the leader's drop from 6,000 to 8,000 m (Clark Field, Darwin); torpedo attacks low and abreast.
SM.79s in vics of three at 4,000 to 6,000 m; torpedo attacks low in pairs.
The Stuka: from about 4,000 m in echelon, each rolling in turn into a 60 to 90 degree dive with its brakes out, bombing at 450 to 700 m and pulling out at about 6 g.

The Il-2's circle (krug): the group circles over the target at 400 to 1,000 m, each diving in turn at 25 to 30 degrees with cannon, rockets and from July 1943 anti-tank bomblets, the circle guarding each one's tail.
Fighter-bombers in 30 to 45 degree dives, bombing at 300 to 900 m; Typhoons and P-47s in a 'cab rank' over Normandy, called down by controllers with the troops.
Fw 190F fighter-bombers in shallow dives and low passes took the Stuka's place.
Dive bombers from 4,000 to 6,000 m in a 70 degree dive with split flaps open, letting go at 450 to 600 m.
The Val from 3,000 to 4,000 m in a 55 to 60 degree dive, letting go at about 450 m.
Torpedo bombers drop low (under 30 m) and slow (about 200 km/h for the American Mk 13); the Japanese anvil: two groups at once from both bows, so a turn away from one meets the other.
